q: Identify the term used to describe a precise sequence of step-by-step instructions to solve a problem.
ms: B — Algorithm. A program is an algorithm implemented in a programming language.

q: Identify the flowchart symbol used to show the start and end of an algorithm.
ms: C — The oval/rounded rectangle is the terminator symbol (START/STOP).

q: Identify the flowchart symbol used to show a decision.
ms: A — Diamond. It has one entry and two labelled exits (Yes/No).

q: Identify the flowchart symbol used for input and output.
ms: B — Parallelogram is used for RECEIVE (input) and SEND (output).

q: Identify the flowchart symbol used to show a process such as a calculation.
ms: D — Rectangle represents a process (assignment or calculation).

q:
A flowchart symbol is drawn as a rectangle with an extra vertical line at each side.

Identify what this symbol represents.
ms: A — The double side-barred rectangle is the sub-process (subprogram) symbol.

q: Identify the construct where instructions are executed one after another in order.
ms: C — Sequence.

q: Identify the construct used when a choice is made between two paths based on a condition.
ms: B — Selection (IF … THEN … ELSE).

q: Identify the construct used to repeat a set of instructions.
ms: A — Iteration (WHILE, REPEAT … UNTIL, FOR).

q: Identify the Edexcel pseudocode statement that stores the value 10 in a variable named `count`.
ms: B — SET count TO 10 is the assignment statement.

q: Identify the pseudocode statement used to display a message to the user.
ms: C — SEND … TO DISPLAY is the Edexcel output statement.

q: Identify the pseudocode statement used to take in a whole number typed by the user.
ms: B — RECEIVE age FROM (INTEGER) KEYBOARD.

q: State the value of `17 MOD 5`.
ms: B — MOD gives the remainder: 17 ÷ 5 = 3 remainder **2**.

q: State the value of `17 DIV 5`.
ms: C — DIV gives whole-number (integer) division: **3**.

q: Identify the expression that is true when `num` is an even number.
ms: C — Even numbers leave remainder 0 when divided by 2.

q: Identify the loop that always executes its instructions at least once.
ms: B — REPEAT … UNTIL tests the condition at the END, so the body always runs at least once.

q: Identify the loop that tests its condition before the instructions are executed.
ms: B — WHILE tests at the start, so the body may run zero times.

q:
A loop must run exactly 20 times.

Identify the most appropriate construct.
ms: C — A FOR loop is count-controlled and is used when the number of repetitions is known.

q: Identify the term for a named memory location whose value can change while a program runs.
ms: B — Variable. A constant cannot change during execution.

q: Identify the term for a value that cannot be changed while a program is running.
ms: C — Constant, e.g. PI.

q: Identify the term for giving a variable its first value, such as `SET total TO 0`.
ms: B — Initialisation.

q: Identify the purpose of a trace table.
options: To translate code into machine code
To record variable values while dry-running an algorithm
ms: B — A trace table records the value of each variable (and output) at each step to determine what the algorithm does and to locate errors.

q:
An algorithm runs without crashing but produces the wrong answer.

Identify the type of error.
ms: C — Logic error: the algorithm executes but the design/logic is wrong.

q: Identify the comparison operator that means 'not equal to' in Edexcel pseudocode.
ms: A — <> means not equal to.

q: Identify which of these is **not** a way of expressing an algorithm in the Edexcel specification.
ms: C — The spec lists written descriptions, flowcharts, pseudocode and program code.

q:
The condition `(score >= 50) AND (score <= 100)` is tested.

Identify the value of `score` that makes the condition true.
ms: C — 50 satisfies both parts: 50 >= 50 is true AND 50 <= 100 is true.

q: Identify what the arrows (flow lines) in a flowchart show.
options: The order in which steps are carried out
ms: B — Flow lines show the order/flow of control.

q:
A flowchart contains an arrow that points back up to an earlier symbol.

Identify the construct this represents.
ms: C — A backwards flow line via a decision creates a loop (iteration).

q: Identify the reason pseudocode cannot be executed by a computer.
options: It is not written in a real programming language
ms: B — Pseudocode is a structured design notation, not an actual programming language, so there is no translator for it.

q:
`NOT (raining)` is evaluated when `raining` is false.

Identify the result.
ms: B — NOT inverts the value: NOT false = true.

q: Describe what is meant by the term 'algorithm'.
ms: A precise sequence of step-by-step instructions (1) to solve a problem / complete a task (1).

q: State **two** ways in which an algorithm can be expressed.
ms: Any two of: written description (1), flowchart (1), pseudocode (1), program code (1).

q: State the purpose of the terminator symbol in a flowchart.
ms: To show where the algorithm starts and stops/ends (1).

q: State the purpose of the decision symbol in a flowchart.
ms: To ask a question / test a condition with two possible exits (Yes/No or True/False) (1).

q: Give **one** advantage of using a flowchart rather than a written description to express an algorithm.
ms: The flow of control / order of steps / decisions and loops can be seen clearly at a glance (1) because standard symbols remove ambiguity of written English (1). Any sensible advantage + expansion.

q: Give **one** advantage of using pseudocode rather than a flowchart to express an algorithm.
ms: Quicker to write / no drawing needed (1) and it is closer to real code so it is easier to convert into a programming language (1).

q: State why pseudocode is not tied to any single programming language.
ms: It is a design notation using structured English / code-like statements, not real syntax, so it can be converted into any language (1).

q: Describe the difference between a variable and a constant.
ms: A variable is a named value/memory location that CAN change while the program runs (1); a constant is a named value that CANNOT change during execution (1).

q: State what is meant by an 'identifier'.
ms: The (unique) name given to a variable / constant / subprogram (1).

q: Explain **one** reason why programmers use meaningful identifier names such as `totalPrice` instead of `x`.
ms: It makes the purpose of the variable clear (1), so the code is easier to read / debug / maintain by the programmer or others (1).

q: State what is meant by 'initialisation'.
ms: Giving a variable a starting value before it is used, e.g. SET total TO 0 (1).

q:
An algorithm adds up ten numbers entered by a user.

State the value the total should be initialised to, and give a reason.
ms: 0 (1), so that the first number added gives a correct running total / no leftover value affects the sum (1).

q: Name the **three** programming constructs and describe each one.
ms: Sequence — instructions carried out one after another in order (1). Selection — a choice between paths based on a condition (IF) (1). Iteration — repeating instructions (loops) (1).

q: Describe the difference between count-controlled and condition-controlled iteration.
ms: Count-controlled repeats a set/known number of times, e.g. FOR loop (1); condition-controlled repeats while/until a condition is met, so the number of repeats is not known in advance, e.g. WHILE or REPEAT UNTIL (1).

q: Describe the difference between a WHILE loop and a REPEAT … UNTIL loop.
ms: WHILE tests the condition at the START so the body may execute zero times (1); REPEAT…UNTIL tests at the END so the body always executes at least once (1). (Also: WHILE repeats while the condition is true; REPEAT repeats until the condition becomes true.)

q: State what is meant by an 'infinite loop'.
ms: A loop whose exit condition is never met, so it repeats forever / never ends (1).

q: Give **one** situation where a REPEAT … UNTIL loop is more appropriate than a FOR loop.
ms: When the number of repetitions is not known in advance (1), e.g. keep asking for a password until it is correct / keep asking for input until it is valid (1).

q: State the purpose of a trace table.
ms: To record the values of variables (and outputs) at each step of an algorithm (1) in order to work out what the algorithm does / to find (logic) errors (1).

q: State what is meant by 'dry running' an algorithm.
ms: Working through the algorithm by hand / on paper, without a computer, recording variable values step by step (1).

q: Describe what a logic error is and how a trace table helps find it.
ms: A logic error is when the algorithm runs but produces the wrong/unexpected result (1); a trace table shows the actual value of each variable at each step, so the step where values go wrong can be identified (1).

q:
Complete this sentence.

An algorithm takes an __________, carries out a __________, and produces an output.
ms: input (1); process (1).

q:
Complete this sentence.

In a flowchart, a rectangle represents a __________ and a parallelogram represents an __________.
ms: process (1); input/output (1).

q:
Complete this sentence.

A __________ loop repeats a known number of times, whereas a __________ -controlled loop repeats until a condition is met.
ms: count-controlled / FOR (1); condition (1).

q:
Draw a straight line (write the matching pairs) to match each term to its meaning.

**Terms:** Sequence, Selection, Iteration
**Meanings:** Repeating code; Making a decision; Instructions in order
ms: Sequence → instructions in order (1). Selection → making a decision (1). Iteration → repeating code (1).

q:
Draw a straight line (write the matching pairs) to match each flowchart symbol to its use.

**Symbols:** Diamond, Parallelogram, Oval
**Uses:** Start/Stop; Decision; Input/Output
ms: Diamond → decision (1). Parallelogram → input/output (1). Oval → start/stop (1).

q:
An algorithm asks a user to enter a temperature and outputs a warning if it is below 0.

State the input to this algorithm.
ms: The temperature (entered by the user) (1).

q:
A vending machine algorithm receives the money inserted and the item code, then dispenses the item and any change.

State **two** inputs to this algorithm.
ms: Money inserted (1); item code/choice (1).

q:
A quiz algorithm keeps a score and displays it at the end, together with a pass/fail message.

State **two** outputs of this algorithm.
ms: The (final) score (1); the pass/fail message (1).

q: Explain why the order of instructions in an algorithm is important.
ms: Instructions are executed in sequence (1); if the order is wrong the result will be wrong / the algorithm will not solve the problem, e.g. outputting a total before it is calculated (1).

q: Explain why an algorithm must be unambiguous.
ms: Each instruction must have exactly one meaning (1) so that it always produces the same, correct result when followed / can be converted into program code without guessing (1).

q: Explain **one** benefit of designing an algorithm before writing program code.
ms: Errors in logic can be found early, e.g. by dry running (1), which saves time/cost compared with fixing them after coding (1). Also accept: gives a clear plan that can be implemented in any language.

q: Explain **one** reason why a programmer would dry run an algorithm with a trace table before coding it.
ms: To check the logic produces the expected output for test data (1) so logic errors are found and corrected before implementation (1).

q: State the output of `SEND 3 + 4 * 2 TO DISPLAY` and give the reason.
ms: 11 (1) because multiplication has higher precedence than addition (BIDMAS), so 4*2 is evaluated first (1).

q:
State the value of each expression.

(i) `29 DIV 6`
(ii) `29 MOD 6`
ms: (i) 4 (1) — whole-number division. (ii) 5 (1) — the remainder.

q:
A variable `n` holds a whole number of seconds.

Write an expression using DIV, and another using MOD, to give the whole minutes and the seconds left over.
ms: Minutes: n DIV 60 (1). Seconds left: n MOD 60 (1).

q:
State whether each condition is true or false when `x = 7`.

(i) `(x > 5) AND (x < 7)`
(ii) `(x > 5) OR (x < 7)`
ms: (i) False — x < 7 is false so AND fails (1). (ii) True — x > 5 is true so OR succeeds (1).

q: State the condition needed to test that `num` is a multiple of 5.
ms: num MOD 5 = 0 (1).

q:
A condition should be true when `age` is between 13 and 19 inclusive.

Write the condition in pseudocode.
ms: (age >= 13) AND (age <= 19) (2 — 1 mark per correct comparison joined with AND).

q: State the purpose of indentation inside IF statements and loops in pseudocode.
ms: To show clearly which statements belong inside the construct / to make the structure readable (1).

q: Explain why a WHILE loop might never execute its body.
ms: The condition is tested before the body runs (1); if the condition is false on the first test, the body is skipped entirely (1).

q: Explain why a REPEAT … UNTIL loop is a risk when validating user input if the condition is written incorrectly.
ms: The body always runs at least once and repeats until the condition is true (1); if the condition can never become true (e.g. wrong comparison), the loop becomes infinite and the program never continues (1).

q:
A flowchart has a decision diamond with only one exit arrow.

Explain why this is an error.
ms: A decision must have two exits (Yes/No or True/False) (1); with one exit the false/true case has no path to follow, so the flowchart is incomplete/ambiguous (1).

q: Explain **one** reason why algorithms shown as flowcharts are useful when explaining a system to non-programmers.
ms: Symbols and arrows show the steps and decisions visually (1) so someone with no coding knowledge can follow the logic (1).

q:
An algorithm finds the largest number in a list.

Explain why a variable often called `highest` is set to the first item of the list (or a very low value) before the loop starts.
ms: It needs a starting value to compare the other items against (1); using the first item / very low value guarantees any larger item will correctly replace it (1).

q: Explain what would happen if a counter variable inside a WHILE loop was never updated.
ms: The loop condition would never change/become false (1), so the loop would repeat forever — an infinite loop (1).

q: State **two** items of information that are recorded in a trace table.
ms: Any two: the value of each variable at each step (1); the output produced (1); the result of condition tests (1); the line/step number (1).

q:
A trace table has a column for the condition of a loop.

Explain why the condition column must be completed for the pass where the loop ends.
ms: The loop only ends when the condition test fails/succeeds on that pass (1); recording it shows why the loop exited and confirms the final variable values are correct (1).

q: Describe the difference between the `=` used in `SET x TO 5` style assignment and the `=` used in a condition such as `IF x = 5`.
ms: Assignment stores/copies a value into a variable (1); in a condition, = compares two values and gives true/false without changing them (1).

q:
An algorithm is described as 'finite'.

Explain what this means and why it matters.
ms: It must come to an end / terminate after a limited number of steps (1); otherwise it would never produce its output/solve the problem (1).

q: Explain the purpose of the condition in an IF … THEN … ELSE statement.
ms: It is evaluated to true or false (1) to decide which branch (THEN part or ELSE part) is executed (1).

q:
An algorithm reads a price, adds 20% tax, and displays the final price.

Identify the input, the process and the output.
ms: Input: the price (1). Process: calculating price + 20% (price * 1.2) (1). Output: displaying the final price (1).

q:
Look at this pseudocode statement.

`SET average TO total / count`

State the construct being used and what the statement does.
ms: Sequence / assignment (a process) (1); it divides total by count and stores the result in average (1).

q: Identify the **two** constructs used in this pseudocode.
code:
WHILE answer <> 'yes' DO
    RECEIVE answer FROM KEYBOARD
END WHILE
SEND 'Thank you' TO DISPLAY
ms: Iteration — the WHILE loop (1); sequence — statements executed in order (the RECEIVE inside, then SEND after) (1).

q: Identify the construct used in this pseudocode and state how many times the loop body executes.
code:
FOR index FROM 1 TO 12 DO
    SEND index * 3 TO DISPLAY
END FOR
ms: Count-controlled iteration / FOR loop (1); the body executes 12 times (1).

q: Identify **two** variables used in this pseudocode.
code:
SET total TO 0
RECEIVE num FROM (INTEGER) KEYBOARD
SET total TO total + num
ms: total (1); num (1).

q:
A programmer writes `SET PI TO 3.14159` and never changes it.

State what PI should be declared as, and give one benefit of doing so.
ms: A constant (1); benefit: it cannot be changed accidentally during execution / the name makes code readable and the value only needs updating in one place (1).

q: Explain why `2totalPrice` would be a poor identifier even if the language allowed it.
ms: Identifiers should be meaningful and follow conventions — starting with a digit is confusing/invalid in most languages (1) and makes code harder to read/maintain or causes syntax errors (1).

q:
An algorithm outputs 'Pass' when a mark is 40 or more, otherwise 'Fail'.

Identify the correct condition for the Pass branch.
ms: B — '40 or more' includes 40, so >= is required. Using > is a classic boundary logic error.

q: Identify which construct this flowchart section represents: a diamond whose 'No' arrow loops back to an earlier input symbol.
ms: C — The backwards arrow makes it a loop (iteration), used here to repeat until input is acceptable.

q:
A trace table is being completed for a loop.

Identify when a new value is written in a variable's column.
options: On every line, even if unchanged
Only when the variable's value changes
Only at the end of the algorithm
Only when the variable is output
ms: B — Values are recorded when they change; repeating unchanged values wastes time and can lose marks for unclear tables.

q: State the final value of `x` after this pseudocode executes, and name the construct used.
code:
SET x TO 4
SET x TO x + 6
SET x TO x DIV 2
ms: x = 5 (1) — (4+6)=10, 10 DIV 2 = 5. Construct: sequence (1).

q: Explain what the statement `SET count TO count + 1` does and where it is commonly used.
ms: It increments count by 1 / adds one to the current value and stores it back (1); commonly used as a counter inside a loop (1).

q:
A student says 'an algorithm and a computer program are the same thing'.

Explain why the student is not correct.
ms: An algorithm is the design — step-by-step instructions that can be written as a description/flowchart/pseudocode (1); a program is the implementation of an algorithm in an actual programming language that a computer can run (1).

q: State **two** properties every well-written algorithm must have.
ms: Any two: unambiguous/precise instructions (1); correct order/sequence (1); finite — must terminate (1); produces the correct output for its inputs (1).

q:
An algorithm for a cash machine: receive card details, receive PIN, check PIN, dispense cash or show error.

Give **one** example each of sequence, selection and a sensible use of iteration in this algorithm.
ms: Sequence: receive card then receive PIN in order (1). Selection: IF PIN correct THEN dispense ELSE error (1). Iteration: repeat PIN entry up to 3 attempts / until correct (1).

q: Explain why test data is needed when dry running an algorithm.
ms: The algorithm must be traced with actual values (1) so the output can be compared with the expected result to confirm correctness / reveal logic errors (1).

q:
A loop should ask for a password until the correct one is entered.

State the most appropriate loop construct and give the reason.
ms: REPEAT … UNTIL (1) because the password must be asked for at least once and the number of attempts is unknown (1). (WHILE with priming input also creditworthy.)

q: State what is output by `SEND 'Total: ' & total TO DISPLAY` when total is 25, and name the string operation used.
ms: Total: 25 (1); concatenation — joining the string and the value (1).

q: Describe the steps a student should follow to complete a trace table for a short algorithm containing a loop.
ms: Make a column for each variable (and output/condition) (1); work through the algorithm line by line, writing values as they change (1); on each loop pass re-test the condition and continue until it exits, recording the final values/output (1).

q:
Discuss the advantages and disadvantages of using pseudocode compared with flowcharts when designing algorithms.

Your answer should consider ease of creation, clarity of control flow, and conversion to program code.
ms: Level-marked. Indicative content — Pseudocode: quick to write with no drawing tools; closely matches real code so conversion is straightforward; easy to edit; but long algorithms can be hard to follow and loops/branches are less visual. Flowcharts: standard symbols make decisions/loops visually obvious; good for non-programmers; but slow to draw, hard to modify, become unwieldy for large algorithms, and are further from code. A balanced answer with justified points on both sides and a conclusion accesses the top level (5–6).
